compelling /kəmˈpel.ɪŋ/ adj. 極具說服力、引人入勝 ⭐⭐⭐⭐
operant conditioning /ˈɒp.ər.ənt kənˈdɪʃ.ən.ɪŋ/ n. 操作制約（心理學名詞） ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

📚 生字詳細解析

1. sophomore year

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈsɒf.ə.mɔː jɪər/ (美音: /ˈsɑː.fə.mɔːr jɪr/)
  • 廣東話解法：美國學制入面，高中或者大學嘅「二年級」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The injury happened on the final day of my sophomore year of high school.
  • 廣東話口語: 單意外發生喺我高中二年級最後嗰日。

2. rolled out of

  • 詞性：片語動詞 (Phrasal Verb)
  • 讀音：/rəʊld aʊt əv/
  • 廣東話解法：從某個地方碌出嚟、跌出嚟（例如跌落床），或者從某個狀態/地方移出。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: He rolled out of bed and rushed to school.
  • 廣東話口語: 佢由張床度碌落嚟（急急腳起身），跟住衝去返學。

3. helipad

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈhel.ɪ.pæd/
  • 廣東話解法：直升機升降嘅空地，即係「直升機停機坪」（通常喺醫院天台或者平地）。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: They wheeled me out of the hospital doors and toward the helipad.
  • 廣東話口語: 佢哋推我出醫院門口，一直推去直升機停機坪嗰邊。

4. stretcher

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈstretʃ.ər/
  • 廣東話解法：急救或者運送傷者用嘅「擔架」或者「擔架床」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The paramedics carefully lifted him onto the stretcher.
  • 廣東話口語: 救護員好小心咁將佢抬上張擔架床度。

5. rattle

  • 詞性：動詞 (Verb) / 名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈræt.əl/
  • 廣東話解法：除咗解作發出「格格聲」，用喺人身上係指「嚇親」、「令到人慌亂」或者「打亂陣腳」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The sudden loud noise really rattled him.
  • 廣東話口語: 突然間一吓巨響，真係嚇親佢（搞到佢六神無主）。

6. seizure

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈsiː.ʒər/
  • 廣東話解法：醫學上指大腦神經異常放電引起嘅「癲癇發作」或者「抽筋」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: Shortly after arriving at the hospital, I had another seizure.
  • 廣東話口語: 去到醫院冇耐，我又發作（抽筋）多咗一次。

7. spinal taps (spinal tap 嘅眾數)

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈspaɪ.nəl tæps/
  • 廣東話解法：腰椎穿刺，俗稱「抽脊髓」，係一種由背脊位抽腦脊液嚟做化驗嘅醫療程序。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The doctors had to perform multiple spinal taps to check for infection.
  • 廣東話口語: 班醫生要做幾次腰椎穿刺（抽脊髓）嚟檢查有冇受感染。

8. biopsies (biopsy 嘅眾數)

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈbaɪ.ɒp.siz/
  • 廣東話解法：活組織抽驗，俗稱「抽針」或者「抽組織化驗」，用嚟檢查細胞有冇病變。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: We are waiting for the results of the biopsies.
  • 廣東話口語: 我哋等緊抽組織化驗嘅結果。

9. Mercifully,

  • 詞性：副詞 (Adverb)
  • 讀音：/ˈmɜː.sɪ.fəl.i/
  • 廣東話解法：帶有極大鬆一口氣嘅感覺，指不幸中之大幸。廣東話通常講「好彩」、「幸好」或者「感恩地」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: Mercifully, my brain swelling began to reduce.
  • 廣東話口語: 好彩（謝天謝地），我個腦嘅腫脹開始退喇。

10. precariously

  • 詞性：副詞 (Adverb)
  • 讀音：/prɪˈkeə.ri.əs.li/
  • 廣東話解法：形容處於一個好危險、唔穩定或者隨時出事嘅狀態。廣東話通常講「搖搖欲墜咁」或者「危危乎」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: His life hung precariously in the balance.
  • 廣東話口語: 佢條命喺生死邊緣危危乎（命懸一線）。

11. ophthalmologist

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˌɒf.θælˈmɒl.ə.dʒɪst/
  • 廣東話解法：眼科醫生（專科）。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: I had to see an ophthalmologist to check my double vision.
  • 廣東話口語: 我要去睇眼科醫生檢查吓我啲重影問題。

12. rolled around

  • 詞性：片語動詞 (Phrasal Verb)
  • 讀音：/rəʊld əˈraʊnd/
  • 廣東話解法：指某個時間、季節或者日子「不經不覺又來到」或者「降臨」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: When spring rolled around, I returned to the baseball field.
  • 廣東話口語: 當春天（不經不覺）嚟到，我又返返去棒球場。

13. varsity

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun) / 形容詞 (Adjective)
  • 讀音：/ˈvɑː.sə.ti/
  • 廣東話解法：中學或大學入面代表學校出賽嘅「校隊」（通常係最頂級嗰隊，次一級會叫 JV - Junior Varsity）。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: He was cut from the varsity baseball team.
  • 廣東話口語: 佢俾棒球校隊（一線隊伍）叮走咗。

14. vividly

  • 詞性：副詞 (Adverb)
  • 讀音：/ˈvɪv.ɪd.li/
  • 廣東話解法：記憶或者畫面非常生動、清晰。廣東話通常講「歷歷在目咁」或者「好清楚咁」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: I still vividly remember the day I got my driver’s license.
  • 廣東話口語: 我依然歷歷在目咁記得我考到車牌嗰日。

15. innings

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈɪn.ɪŋz/
  • 廣東話解法：棒球或者板球比賽入面嘅「局」（例如第一局、第九局）。留意英文入面單數同眾數都係有 “s” 尾。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: I only played a total of 11 innings that year.
  • 廣東話口語: 嗰年我總共只係打咗 11 局。

16. lackluster

  • 詞性：形容詞 (Adjective)
  • 讀音：/ˈlækˌlʌs.tər/
  • 廣東話解法：字面係失去光澤，比喻表現好平庸、無動力或者令人提不起勁。廣東話講「表現平平」、「乏善可陳」或者「毫無光彩」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: Despite his hard work, he had a lackluster season.
  • 廣東話口語: 雖然佢好勤力，但佢成季嘅表現都係平平無奇（乏善可陳）。

17. rippled

  • 詞性：動詞 (Verb 過去式)
  • 讀音：/ˈrɪp.əld/
  • 廣東話解法：原意係水面起漣漪。引申指某種感覺或者影響好似波浪咁擴散、蔓延。廣東話講「起漣漪」、「蔓延」或者「擴散」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: A sense of relief rippled through the crowd.
  • 廣東話口語: 一種鬆一口氣嘅感覺喺人群之中蔓延開去。

18. compelling

  • 詞性：形容詞 (Adjective)
  • 讀音：/kəmˈpel.ɪŋ/
  • 廣東話解法：理由或者故事非常有說服力、吸引人，令人不得不信或者不得不注意。廣東話講「極具說服力」或者「引人入勝」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The book provides compelling evidence for its theory.
  • 廣東話口語: 本書為佢嘅理論提供咗極具說服力嘅證據。

19. operant conditioning

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈɒp.ər.ənt kənˈdɪʃ.ən.ɪŋ/
  • 廣東話解法：心理學專有名詞，中文譯做「操作制約」或「操作性條件反射」。簡單嚟講就係透過獎勵（增強）同懲罰去改變行為嘅學習過程。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: We learned about B.F. Skinner and his experiments on operant conditioning.
  • 廣東話口語: 我哋學咗斯金納（B.F. Skinner）同埋佢關於操作制約嘅實驗。

item.title: 3. Flexible Arguments
item.description:
Flexible Classes with *args and **kwargs

Sometimes, when you build a class, you don’t know exactly how much information the user will provide.

Imagine creating a Pizza class.

One customer might order:

Medium + Extra Cheese

while another customer might order:

Large + Pepperoni + Sausage + Onions + Peppers

It would be inconvenient to create a separate parameter for every possible topping.

Python gives us two powerful tools for handling an unlimited number of arguments:

  • *args
  • **kwargs

The magic is in the asterisks (* and **).

The names args and kwargs are simply common naming conventions. They are not special keywords.

For example, these work the same way:

*args
*toppings
*items

and:

**kwargs
**options
**settings

The asterisks are what matter.

1. *args — The Grab Bag

*args allows you to pass any number of regular, unnamed arguments to a function or class.

Python collects all those extra arguments and stores them in a tuple.

A tuple is similar to a list, except that its contents cannot normally be changed after it is created.

Think of *args like calling out pizza toppings:

“Pepperoni, onions, olives!”

These are individual values without labels.

Example: Pizza with Any Number of Toppings

class Pizza:

    # size is required.
    # *args catches all additional unnamed arguments.
    def __init__(self, size, *args):
        self.size = size
        self.toppings = args

    def describe(self):
        print(f"A {self.size} pizza with:")

        for topping in self.toppings:
            print(f"- {topping}")


# One topping
cheese_pizza = Pizza("Medium", "Extra Cheese")


# Four toppings
supreme = Pizza(
    "Large",
    "Pepperoni",
    "Sausage",
    "Onions",
    "Peppers"
)

supreme.describe()

The *args parameter collects the toppings into a tuple.

Conceptually:

args
 ↓
("Pepperoni", "Sausage", "Onions", "Peppers")

The output would be:

A Large pizza with:
- Pepperoni
- Sausage
- Onions
- Peppers

2. **kwargs — The Custom Order Form

**kwargs stands for Keyword Arguments.

It allows you to pass any number of labeled arguments using the name=value format.

Python collects these labeled values into a dictionary.

Think of **kwargs as filling out a custom order form:

crust = thin
sauce = spicy
well_done = True

Each value has a label, or key.

Example: A Flexible Smartphone Class

class SmartPhone:

    # brand is required.
    # **kwargs catches all custom specifications.
    def __init__(self, brand, **kwargs):
        self.brand = brand

        # kwargs is a dictionary.
        self.specs = kwargs

    def show_specs(self):
        print(f"--- {self.brand} Phone ---")

        for key, value in self.specs.items():
            print(f"{key}: {value}")


# We can provide any number of custom specifications.
my_phone = SmartPhone(
    "Apple",
    storage="256GB",
    color="Midnight",
    has_headphone_jack=False
)

my_phone.show_specs()

Conceptually, kwargs contains:

{
    "storage": "256GB",
    "color": "Midnight",
    "has_headphone_jack": False
}

The output would be:

--- Apple Phone ---
storage: 256GB
color: Midnight
has_headphone_jack: False

The key advantage is flexibility.

We don’t have to predict every possible specification when we create the class.

Putting *args and **kwargs Together

You can use both *args and **kwargs in the same class.

However, Python requires them to appear in a specific order.

The general pattern is:

  1. Regular required parameters
  2. *args
  3. **kwargs

Think of it as:

Required → Unnamed extras → Named extras

Example: Video Game Character

class VideoGameCharacter:

    def __init__(self, name, *args, **kwargs):
        self.name = name
        self.inventory = args
        self.stats = kwargs


hero = VideoGameCharacter(
    "Link",

    # *args
    "Sword",
    "Shield",

    # **kwargs
    health=100,
    magic=50
)

The information is stored like this:

name
 ↓
"Link"

inventory
 ↓
("Sword", "Shield")

stats
 ↓
{
    "health": 100,
    "magic": 50
}

So one object can contain three different types of information:

VideoGameCharacter
        │
        ├── name
        │     └── "Link"
        │
        ├── inventory
        │     └── ("Sword", "Shield")
        │
        └── stats
              ├── health = 100
              └── magic = 50

This makes classes extremely flexible.

*args vs. **kwargs

It is helpful to compare the two directly.

Feature *args **kwargs
Accepts Extra unnamed arguments Extra named arguments
Stored as Tuple Dictionary
Example "Sword", "Shield" health=100, magic=50
Think of it as A grab bag A custom order form
Asterisk * **

For example:

*args

might collect:

("Sword", "Shield", "Potion")

while:

**kwargs

might collect:

{
    "health": 100,
    "magic": 50,
    "level": 10
}

The Big Picture: Making Flexible Classes

We have now seen several ways to make classes flexible.

Required attributes

These must be provided:

def __init__(self, name, age):

Optional attributes with default values

These can be omitted:

def __init__(self, name, age=0):

Optional information using None

This represents information that may not exist:

def __init__(self, name, phone=None):

Unlimited unnamed information with *args

def __init__(self, name, *items):

Unlimited named information with **kwargs

def __init__(self, name, **options):

All together

def __init__(self, name, age=0, *args, **kwargs):

This gives us a powerful range of possibilities for designing classes.

A Real-World Example: Bank Accounts

Let’s apply everything we’ve learned to a practical example.

A bank account is something we can easily understand in the real world.

A bank account has:

Attributes — What the account has

  • Owner’s name
  • Current balance

Methods — What the account can do

  • Deposit money
  • Withdraw money
  • Check the balance

Let’s build a BankAccount class step by step.

Step 1: Create the Blueprint

First, we define our class and its constructor.

class BankAccount:

    # Create a new account
    def __init__(self, owner, starting_balance=0.0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = starting_balance

The parameter:

starting_balance=0.0

provides a default value.

Therefore, if someone creates an account without specifying a starting balance, the account automatically starts with $0.00.

For example:

alice_account = BankAccount("Alice", 100.0)

Alice starts with $100.

But:

bob_account = BankAccount("Bob")

Bob starts with $0.

Step 2: Add Methods

Now let’s teach our BankAccount class how to handle money.

We will create three methods:

  1. deposit()
  2. withdraw()
  3. check_balance()
class BankAccount:

    def __init__(self, owner, starting_balance=0.0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = starting_balance

    # ACTION 1: Deposit money
    def deposit(self, amount):

        if amount > 0:
            self.balance += amount
            print(
                f"Deposited ${amount}. "
                f"New balance is ${self.balance}."
            )
        else:
            print("You must deposit a positive amount!")

    # ACTION 2: Withdraw money
    def withdraw(self, amount):

        # Make sure there is enough money
        if amount > self.balance:
            print(
                f"Declined! You only have "
                f"${self.balance} in your account."
            )

        elif amount <= 0:
            print("You must withdraw a positive amount!")

        else:
            self.balance -= amount
            print(
                f"Withdrew ${amount}. "
                f"New balance is ${self.balance}."
            )

    # ACTION 3: Check the balance
    def check_balance(self):
        print(
            f"Account Owner: {self.owner} | "
            f"Current Balance: ${self.balance}"
        )

Notice that every method has self as its first parameter.

This is necessary because each method needs to know which particular bank account it is working with.

For example:

self.balance

means:

“The balance belonging to this particular account.”

Step 3: Create and Test Our Objects

Our blueprint is now complete.

Let’s create some actual bank account objects and test them.

# Create an account for Alice with $100
alice_account = BankAccount("Alice", 100.0)

# Create an account for Bob with $0
bob_account = BankAccount("Bob")

We now have two separate objects:

BankAccount class
       ↓
 ┌─────┴─────┐
 ↓           ↓
Alice       Bob
$100         $0

Let’s make some transactions.

# Alice deposits $50
alice_account.deposit(50)
# Deposited $50. New balance is $150.0.

# Alice withdraws $20
alice_account.withdraw(20)
# Withdrew $20. New balance is $130.0.

Now let’s see what happens when Bob tries to withdraw more money than he has.

bob_account.withdraw(500)
# Declined! You only have $0.0 in your account.

Finally, let’s check both accounts.

alice_account.check_balance()
# Account Owner: Alice | Current Balance: $130.0

bob_account.check_balance()
# Account Owner: Bob | Current Balance: $0.0

Putting Everything Together

Our BankAccount class combines data and actions into one organized structure.

                 BankAccount
                      │
          ┌───────────┴───────────┐
          │                       │
      Attributes               Methods
          │                       │
    ┌─────┴─────┐        ┌────────┼────────┐
    │           │        │        │        │
  owner      balance   deposit  withdraw  check_balance

Each object created from the class has its own attributes.

alice_account.owner
# Alice

alice_account.balance
# 130.0

while:

bob_account.owner
# Bob

bob_account.balance
# 0.0

The same class can therefore be used to create as many independent bank accounts as we need.

item.title: English Word Dictionary Day 4
item.description:
Note

💡 使用說明：此字典專為廣東話使用者而設，提供地道廣東話解釋、句式文法拆解同埋口語翻譯。

🔍 內容快速索引

✍️ 實用句式 (Sentence Patterns)

  1. ... though they clearly were, ... (倒裝讓步句式)
  2. What is it about [X] that [Y]? (疑問強調句式)
  3. It is in [X] that [Y]. (分裂強調句)
  4. lie in wait... at the drop of a hat (連續動作/俚語組合)

📚 重點生字 (Vocabulary)

英文生字 音標 (IPA) 詞性 廣東話地道意思
renounce /rɪˈnaʊns/ v. 放棄、聲明決裂、拒絕承認
uphold /ʌpˈhəʊld/ v. 維護、捍衛、堅持
necessitates /nəˈses.ɪ.teɪts/ v. 令…成為必要、迫使
bootstraps /ˈbuːt.stræps/ n. 自力更生、靠自己雙手
amid /əˈmɪd/ prep. 喺…之中、喺…氣氛/環境下
tie up the loose ends /taɪ ʌp ðə luːs endz/ idiom 執手尾、搞掂剩低嘅細節
outset /ˈaʊt.set/ n. 開端、一開始
scorn /skɔːn/ n. / v. 輕蔑、鄙視、嘲笑
perilous /ˈper.əl.əs/ adj. 極度危險嘅
a dig at me /ə dɪɡ ət miː/ idiom 單打我、挖苦/暗寸我
berated /bɪˈreɪ.tɪd/ v. 痛斥、狂鬧、嚴厲責罵
steeped /stiːpt/ adj. 沉浸於、充滿住 (steeped in)
schema /ˈskiː.mə/ n. 基模、認知架構、既定模式
triumph over /ˈtraɪ.əmf ˈəʊ.vər/ phr. v. 戰勝、擊敗、克服
ample /ˈæm.pəl/ adj. 充足、大量、大把
coolheaded /ˌkuːlˈhed.ɪd/ adj. 冷靜嘅、臨危不亂嘅
pent-up /ˌpentˈʌp/ adj. 壓抑嘅、鬱積嘅 (情緒)

🧠 實用句式解析 (Sentence Patterns)

1. 倒裝讓步句式

原文：Psychology keywords though they clearly were, the truths they contained differed greatly from the youth’s imagined meanings.

  • 文法拆解：呢度用咗倒裝句 [名詞/形容詞] + though + [主語] + [動詞]，語氣上比普通的 “Although they were clearly psychology keywords” 更強烈，用嚟強調最前面嗰個字眼（心理學關鍵字）。
  • 廣東話翻譯：雖然呢啲的確係心理學嘅關鍵字，但裡面包含嘅真相同個後生仔想像嘅意思有好大出入。
  • 應用例子：Hard though it was, we finished the project. (雖然好難，但我哋都完成咗個項目。)

2. 疑問強調句式

原文：What is it about all this that I’m having a hard time accepting?

  • 文法拆解：What is it about [X] that [Y]? 係一個好靚嘅強調句型。你唔係單純問 “Why can’t I accept this?”，而係深究「究竟 X 入面有啲咩特質，搞到 Y 咁樣？」
  • 廣東話翻譯：究竟呢一切入面有啲咩，令到我咁難去接受？
  • 應用例子：What is it about him that makes everyone angry? (究竟佢個人有啲咩特質，搞到個個都咁嬲？)

3. 分裂強調句 (Cleft Sentence)

原文：It is in trying to progress past who one is now that there is value.

  • 文法拆解：It is [強調部分] that [剩餘部分]。作者想強調「價值」並唔係存在於結果，而係存在於「嘗試超越自我」呢個過程之中。
  • 廣東話翻譯：價值正正係存在於「努力去超越現在嘅自己」呢個過程之中。

4. 俚語連續動作組合

原文：lie in wait for any opening and attack at the drop of a hat.

  • 文法拆解：呢句由兩個生動嘅片語組成。lie in wait 指埋伏、伺機而動；at the drop of a hat 指一有信號就即刻做（毫不猶豫）。
  • 廣東話翻譯：（佢哋）伏擊等緊任何破綻，一有機會就毫不猶豫咁（一觸即發）發動攻擊。

📚 生字詳細解析 (Vocabulary)

1. renounce /rɪˈnaʊns/ (v.)

  • 廣東話解法：正式宣佈放棄（信仰、權利或行為），或者聲明決裂。口語通常講「放棄」、「唔再要」或者「割席」。
  • 例句：He decided to renounce his former beliefs. (佢決定放棄佢以前嘅信仰。)

2. uphold /ʌpˈhəʊld/ (v.)

  • 廣東話解法：支持或者維護（法律、決定或原則）。口語通常講「力撐」、「維持」或者「捍衛」。
  • 例句：We will uphold the law at all costs. (我哋會不惜一切捍衛法律。)

3. necessitates /nəˈses.ɪ.teɪts/ (v.)

  • 廣東話解法：令到某樣嘢變成必需。口語通常講「迫使」或者「無可避免要…」。
  • 例句：The new rules necessitate a change in our strategy. (新嘅規矩迫使我哋必須改變策略。)

4. bootstraps /ˈbuːt.stræps/ (n.)

  • 廣東話解法：「Bootstraps」（靴襻/拔靴帶）原意指靴子後方的拉環。指唔靠外力，單靠自己雙手同努力去改善處境。口語講「自力更生」、「靠自己捱出頭」。
  • 例句：He built his business by his bootstraps. (佢靠自己雙手白手興家。)

5. amid /əˈmɪd/ (prep.)

  • 廣東話解法：被…包圍，或者處於某種氣氛/環境之中。口語通常講「喺…之中」或者「喺…氣氛下」。
  • 例句：He resigned amid rumors of corruption. (佢喺貪污嘅謠言聲之中辭職。)

6. tie up the loose ends (idiom)

  • 廣東話解法：處理埋剩低未搞掂嘅小問題或者細節。口語通常講「執手尾」、「搞埋啲手尾」或者「跟進埋啲蘇州屎」。
  • 例句：We just need to tie up a few loose ends before launching the product. (推出產品之前，我哋淨係要執埋少少手尾就得。)

7. outset /ˈaʊt.set/ (n.)

  • 廣東話解法：事情的開端、開始。通常用 at/from the outset。口語講「一開始」或者「開頭」。
  • 例句：I told him from the outset that it wouldn’t work. (我一開始已經同佢講咗咁樣係行唔通嘅。)

8. scorn /skɔːn/ (n. / v.)

  • 廣東話解法：強烈嘅輕蔑或者鄙視。口語講「睇唔起」、「奚落」或者「不屑」。
  • 例句：She looked at him with scorn. (佢用好鄙視嘅眼神望住佢。)

9. perilous /ˈper.əl.əs/ (adj.)

  • 廣東話解法：充滿危險嘅。口語講「極度危險」或者「步步驚心」。
  • 例句：The journey through the jungle was perilous. (穿越叢林嘅旅程極度危險。)

10. a dig at me (idiom)

  • 廣東話解法：對某人作出嘲諷或者挖苦。口語講「單打我」、「暗寸我」或者「潤我」。
  • 例句：Was that remark a dig at me? (頭先嗰句話係咪暗寸緊我？)

11. berated /bɪˈreɪ.tɪd/ (v. 過去式)

  • 廣東話解法：嚴厲咁責罵某人。口語講「狂鬧」、「鬧到一面屁」或者「痛斥」。
  • 例句：The boss berated him for his mistake. (老闆因為佢個失誤狂鬧佢。)

12. steeped /stiːpt/ (adj.)

  • 廣東話解法：通常配搭 steeped in，指深深沉浸喺某種事物之中（如歷史、傳統）。口語講「浸淫喺」、「充滿住」。
  • 例句：The city is steeped in history. (呢個城市充滿住濃厚嘅歷史氣息。)

13. schema /ˈskiː.mə/ (n.)

  • 廣東話解法：心理學術語，指人腦中組織知識嘅「基模」或者圖式。口語可以理解為「既定模式」、「認知框架」。
  • 例句：Our schema affects how we process new information. (我哋嘅認知框架會影響我哋點樣處理新資訊。)

14. triumph over /ˈtraɪ.əmf ˈəʊ.vər/ (phr. v.)

  • 廣東話解法：經過巨大努力後戰勝困難或敵人。口語講「戰勝」、「克服」或者「贏咗」。
  • 例句：She finally triumphed over her illness. (佢最終戰勝咗病魔。)

15. ample /ˈæm.pəl/ (adj.)

  • 廣東話解法：數量上非常足夠。口語講「充足」、「大把」或者「好夠」。
  • 例句：We have ample time to prepare. (我哋有大把時間準備。)

16. coolheaded /ˌkuːlˈhed.ɪd/ (adj.)

  • 廣東話解法：喺緊急或困難情況下保持頭腦清醒。口語講「冷靜」、「臨危不亂」。
  • 例句：You need to remain coolheaded during a crisis. (危機發生嗰陣你需要保持臨危不亂。)

17. pent-up /ˌpentˈʌp/ (adj.)

  • 廣東話解法：通常用嚟形容被壓抑咗好耐無法釋放嘅情緒或力量。口語講「壓抑咗好耐」、「屈住屈住」。
  • 例句：He screamed to release his pent-up frustration. (佢大聲叫出嚟，釋放壓抑咗好耐嘅挫敗感。)

item.title: 2. Optional Attributes
item.description:
Optional Attributes

An optional attribute simply means that when you create a new object, you don’t have to provide that particular piece of information.

If you leave it out, Python uses a default value instead.

We actually used an optional attribute earlier in our BankAccount example.

Consider:

def __init__(self, owner, starting_balance=0.0):

Here:

  • owner is required.
  • starting_balance is optional.
  • If no starting balance is provided, Python uses 0.0.

For example:

alice_account = BankAccount("Alice", 100.0)

Alice starts with $100.

But:

bob_account = BankAccount("Bob")

Bob automatically starts with $0.

This is the basic idea behind optional attributes.

1. The “Default Value” Method

The most straightforward way to create an optional attribute is to give the parameter a default value inside __init__.

You use the equals sign (=) to specify the default.

class Dog:

    # name is REQUIRED.
    # collar_color is OPTIONAL and defaults to "Red".
    def __init__(self, name, collar_color="Red"):
        self.name = name
        self.collar_color = collar_color


# We only provide the name.
# Python automatically uses "Red".
dog_1 = Dog("Buddy")

print(f"{dog_1.name} has a {dog_1.collar_color} collar.")
# Buddy has a Red collar.


# We provide both values.
# Python uses "Blue" instead of the default.
dog_2 = Dog("Daisy", "Blue")

print(f"{dog_2.name} has a {dog_2.collar_color} collar.")
# Daisy has a Blue collar.

The important idea is:

collar_color="Red"

means:

“If the user doesn’t provide a collar color, use Red.”

But if the user does provide a value:

Dog("Daisy", "Blue")

Python uses "Blue" instead.

2. The None Method — When Information Is Missing

Sometimes an attribute is optional because the information might not exist yet.

In Python, we can use the special value None to represent:

“There is currently no value.”

For example, imagine creating a user profile where a phone number is optional.

class UserProfile:

    # phone_number is optional.
    # If no number is provided, it is set to None.
    def __init__(self, username, phone_number=None):
        self.username = username
        self.phone_number = phone_number

    def show_profile(self):
        print(f"User: {self.username}")

        # Check whether a phone number was provided.
        if self.phone_number is None:
            print("Phone: No number provided.")
        else:
            print(f"Phone: {self.phone_number}")


# Create a user without a phone number
user_1 = UserProfile("CoolSkater99")

user_1.show_profile()

The output would be:

User: CoolSkater99
Phone: No number provided.

Here, None doesn’t mean that the phone number is zero or an empty string.

It means:

“No phone number has been provided.”

⚠️ The Golden Rule of Optional Attributes

When defining your __init__ method, all required parameters must come before optional parameters.

✅ Correct

def __init__(self, name, age, color="Brown"):

Here:

  • name is required.
  • age is required.
  • color is optional.

❌ Incorrect

def __init__(self, color="Brown", name, age):

This causes a SyntaxError because Python does not allow a required parameter to appear after a parameter with a default value.

A simple rule to remember is:

Required first, optional last.

item.title: 1. Classes in Python: A Beginner’s Guide to Object-Oriented Programming
item.description:
Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming with Python

Welcome to the world of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)!

The name may sound complicated, but the basic idea is quite simple: OOP is a way of organizing programs by modeling things as objects, similar to the way we think about objects in the real world.

A helpful way to understand OOP is to imagine a cookie cutter.

  • A Class is the cookie cutter. It is a blueprint or template that describes what something should look like and what it can do. You cannot eat the cookie cutter, but it determines the shape of every cookie you make.
  • An Object is the cookie. It is an actual thing created from the class. One cookie cutter can be used to make many different cookies.

For example, one Dog class can be used to create many different dog objects:

Dog class
   ↓
 ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
 ↓         ↓         ↓
Buddy     Daisy     Max

Each object follows the same blueprint but can have its own data.

The 4 Key OOP Vocabulary Words

Before writing code, let’s learn four terms that you will encounter constantly when working with classes.

Term Simple Meaning Real-World Example
Class A blueprint or template for creating objects. The general idea of a “Dog”
Object (Instance) A specific item created from a class. Your pet dog, Fido
Attribute Data stored inside an object that describes it. Name, breed, age, fur color
Method A function inside a class that describes an action. Barking, sitting, fetching

A useful way to remember the difference is:

Attributes describe what an object has. Methods describe what an object can do.

Building Our First Class

Let’s turn the general idea of a Dog into Python code.

We want our Dog class to have:

  • Attributes: a name and an age
  • Method: the ability to bark
class Dog:

    # The constructor: used to initialize a new object
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    # A method: an action the dog can perform
    def bark(self):
        print(f"{self.name} says Woof!")

Breaking Down the Code

Let’s examine the code one piece at a time.

1. class Dog:

class Dog:

This tells Python:

“I want to create a new blueprint called Dog.”

By convention, Python class names usually begin with a capital letter.

2. def __init__(self, name, age):

def __init__(self, name, age):

__init__ is a special method called the constructor.

It runs automatically whenever we create a new object from the class.

The constructor allows us to provide the initial information needed to set up our object.

For example:

Dog("Buddy", 3)

Python uses "Buddy" as the name and 3 as the age when setting up the new dog.

3. self.name = name

self.name = name
self.age = age

The keyword self refers to the particular object currently being created or used.

So:

self.name = name

can be understood as:

“Take the name provided by the user and store it as the name of this specific dog.”

Similarly:

self.age = age

means:

“Store this age as the age of this specific dog.”

4. def bark(self):

def bark(self):
    print(f"{self.name} says Woof!")

This is a function defined inside a class, so we call it a method.

The method also receives self because the dog needs to know which dog is performing the action.

Bringing the Class to Life

Our class is only a blueprint so far.

Now let’s use it to create actual objects.

# Create the first dog
dog_1 = Dog("Buddy", 3)

# Create a second dog
dog_2 = Dog("Daisy", 5)

We have now created two separate objects:

  • dog_1 represents Buddy, who is 3 years old.
  • dog_2 represents Daisy, who is 5 years old.

Both objects were created from the same Dog class, but each object has its own data.

Accessing Attributes and Methods

We can interact with an object using the dot operator (.).

Accessing Attributes

print(dog_1.name)
# Buddy

print(dog_2.age)
# 5

The dot tells Python which attribute belonging to the object we want to access.

Calling Methods

dog_1.bark()
# Buddy says Woof!

dog_2.bark()
# Daisy says Woof!

Notice how the same method can produce different results depending on the object that calls it.

This is one of the key ideas behind OOP.

Why Do We Use Classes?

For a very small program, you may not need classes.

For example, if you are writing a quick program to calculate your taxes, a class might be unnecessary.

However, as programs become larger—such as:

  • video games,
  • web applications,
  • data dashboards,
  • simulations, or
  • business software,

classes can make your code much easier to organize.

Imagine a video game with two players.

Without classes, you might have variables such as:

player_1_health
player_1_score
player_2_health
player_2_score

As the game becomes more complicated, you could end up with dozens or even hundreds of related variables.

Instead, we can create a Player class and then create multiple player objects from it.

Player class
      ↓
 ┌────┴────┐
 ↓         ↓
Player 1  Player 2

Each player object can keep track of its own health, score, name, and other information.

A class lets us organize related data and actions into one reusable structure.

Understanding self

The keyword self is one of the most important concepts for beginners learning Python classes.

Think of a class as a blueprint for building robots.

Suppose we use the blueprint to build two robots:

Robot class
     ↓
 ┌───┴────┐
 ↓        ↓
Wall-E   R2-D2

Both robots are built from exactly the same blueprint.

However, if we ask Wall-E to introduce itself, we want Wall-E to give its name—not R2-D2.

In Python, self means:

“this particular object”

or, more casually:

“me” / “my”

Let’s see this in action.

class Robot:

    # self.name means "MY name"
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    # self.name means "MY name"
    def introduce(self):
        print(f"Hello, my name is {self.name}.")


# Create two different robot objects
robot_1 = Robot("Wall-E")
robot_2 = Robot("R2-D2")


robot_1.introduce()
# Hello, my name is Wall-E.

robot_2.introduce()
# Hello, my name is R2-D2.

Even though both robots use exactly the same class definition, each object stores its own name.

robot_1.name → "Wall-E"
robot_2.name → "R2-D2"

That’s the power of self.

What Happens If You Forget self?

One of the most common mistakes beginners make is forgetting self when defining a method.

Consider this example:

class Robot:

    # Oops! We forgot self.
    def beep():
        print("Beep boop!")


my_robot = Robot()
my_robot.beep()

Python will produce an error similar to:

TypeError: Robot.beep() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given

At first, this error can seem strange.

You might think:

“I didn’t give beep() any arguments! The parentheses are empty!”

So where did the mysterious 1 argument come from?

Python Is Doing Something Behind the Scenes

When you write:

my_robot.beep()

Python effectively treats this as:

Robot.beep(my_robot)

In other words, Python automatically passes the object that called the method as the first argument.

That object needs somewhere to go.

That is why we write:

def beep(self):

The self parameter is the place where Python passes the current object.

You can think of it like this:

my_robot.beep()
      ↓
Python automatically passes my_robot
      ↓
Robot.beep(my_robot)
      ↓
             self
              ↓
        "this robot"

So when you forget self, Python is essentially saying:

“I tried to give you the robot object, but your method doesn’t have a parameter to receive it!”

rolled out of /rəʊld aʊt əv/ phr. v. 從…碌出嚟、跌落嚟 ⭐⭐

seizure /ˈsiː.ʒər/ n. 癲癇發作、抽筋 ⭐⭐⭐⭐

compelling /kəmˈpel.ɪŋ/ adj. 極具說服力、引人入勝 ⭐⭐⭐⭐
operant conditioning /ˈɒp.ər.ənt kənˈdɪʃ.ən.ɪŋ/ n. 操作制約（心理學名詞） ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

📚 生字詳細解析

1. sophomore year

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈsɒf.ə.mɔː jɪər/ (美音: /ˈsɑː.fə.mɔːr jɪr/)
  • 廣東話解法：美國學制入面，高中或者大學嘅「二年級」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The injury happened on the final day of my sophomore year of high school.
  • 廣東話口語: 單意外發生喺我高中二年級最後嗰日。

2. rolled out of

  • 詞性：片語動詞 (Phrasal Verb)
  • 讀音：/rəʊld aʊt əv/
  • 廣東話解法：從某個地方碌出嚟、跌出嚟（例如跌落床），或者從某個狀態/地方移出。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: He rolled out of bed and rushed to school.
  • 廣東話口語: 佢由張床度碌落嚟（急急腳起身），跟住衝去返學。

3. helipad

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈhel.ɪ.pæd/
  • 廣東話解法：直升機升降嘅空地，即係「直升機停機坪」（通常喺醫院天台或者平地）。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: They wheeled me out of the hospital doors and toward the helipad.
  • 廣東話口語: 佢哋推我出醫院門口，一直推去直升機停機坪嗰邊。

4. stretcher

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈstretʃ.ər/
  • 廣東話解法：急救或者運送傷者用嘅「擔架」或者「擔架床」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The paramedics carefully lifted him onto the stretcher.
  • 廣東話口語: 救護員好小心咁將佢抬上張擔架床度。

5. rattle

  • 詞性：動詞 (Verb) / 名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈræt.əl/
  • 廣東話解法：除咗解作發出「格格聲」，用喺人身上係指「嚇親」、「令到人慌亂」或者「打亂陣腳」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The sudden loud noise really rattled him.
  • 廣東話口語: 突然間一吓巨響，真係嚇親佢（搞到佢六神無主）。

6. seizure

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈsiː.ʒər/
  • 廣東話解法：醫學上指大腦神經異常放電引起嘅「癲癇發作」或者「抽筋」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: Shortly after arriving at the hospital, I had another seizure.
  • 廣東話口語: 去到醫院冇耐，我又發作（抽筋）多咗一次。

7. spinal taps (spinal tap 嘅眾數)

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈspaɪ.nəl tæps/
  • 廣東話解法：腰椎穿刺，俗稱「抽脊髓」，係一種由背脊位抽腦脊液嚟做化驗嘅醫療程序。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The doctors had to perform multiple spinal taps to check for infection.
  • 廣東話口語: 班醫生要做幾次腰椎穿刺（抽脊髓）嚟檢查有冇受感染。

8. biopsies (biopsy 嘅眾數)

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈbaɪ.ɒp.siz/
  • 廣東話解法：活組織抽驗，俗稱「抽針」或者「抽組織化驗」，用嚟檢查細胞有冇病變。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: We are waiting for the results of the biopsies.
  • 廣東話口語: 我哋等緊抽組織化驗嘅結果。

9. Mercifully,

  • 詞性：副詞 (Adverb)
  • 讀音：/ˈmɜː.sɪ.fəl.i/
  • 廣東話解法：帶有極大鬆一口氣嘅感覺，指不幸中之大幸。廣東話通常講「好彩」、「幸好」或者「感恩地」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: Mercifully, my brain swelling began to reduce.
  • 廣東話口語: 好彩（謝天謝地），我個腦嘅腫脹開始退喇。

10. precariously

  • 詞性：副詞 (Adverb)
  • 讀音：/prɪˈkeə.ri.əs.li/
  • 廣東話解法：形容處於一個好危險、唔穩定或者隨時出事嘅狀態。廣東話通常講「搖搖欲墜咁」或者「危危乎」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: His life hung precariously in the balance.
  • 廣東話口語: 佢條命喺生死邊緣危危乎（命懸一線）。

11. ophthalmologist

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˌɒf.θælˈmɒl.ə.dʒɪst/
  • 廣東話解法：眼科醫生（專科）。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: I had to see an ophthalmologist to check my double vision.
  • 廣東話口語: 我要去睇眼科醫生檢查吓我啲重影問題。

12. rolled around

  • 詞性：片語動詞 (Phrasal Verb)
  • 讀音：/rəʊld əˈraʊnd/
  • 廣東話解法：指某個時間、季節或者日子「不經不覺又來到」或者「降臨」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: When spring rolled around, I returned to the baseball field.
  • 廣東話口語: 當春天（不經不覺）嚟到，我又返返去棒球場。

13. varsity

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun) / 形容詞 (Adjective)
  • 讀音：/ˈvɑː.sə.ti/
  • 廣東話解法：中學或大學入面代表學校出賽嘅「校隊」（通常係最頂級嗰隊，次一級會叫 JV - Junior Varsity）。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: He was cut from the varsity baseball team.
  • 廣東話口語: 佢俾棒球校隊（一線隊伍）叮走咗。

14. vividly

  • 詞性：副詞 (Adverb)
  • 讀音：/ˈvɪv.ɪd.li/
  • 廣東話解法：記憶或者畫面非常生動、清晰。廣東話通常講「歷歷在目咁」或者「好清楚咁」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: I still vividly remember the day I got my driver’s license.
  • 廣東話口語: 我依然歷歷在目咁記得我考到車牌嗰日。

15. innings

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈɪn.ɪŋz/
  • 廣東話解法：棒球或者板球比賽入面嘅「局」（例如第一局、第九局）。留意英文入面單數同眾數都係有 “s” 尾。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: I only played a total of 11 innings that year.
  • 廣東話口語: 嗰年我總共只係打咗 11 局。

16. lackluster

  • 詞性：形容詞 (Adjective)
  • 讀音：/ˈlækˌlʌs.tər/
  • 廣東話解法：字面係失去光澤，比喻表現好平庸、無動力或者令人提不起勁。廣東話講「表現平平」、「乏善可陳」或者「毫無光彩」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: Despite his hard work, he had a lackluster season.
  • 廣東話口語: 雖然佢好勤力，但佢成季嘅表現都係平平無奇（乏善可陳）。

17. rippled

  • 詞性：動詞 (Verb 過去式)
  • 讀音：/ˈrɪp.əld/
  • 廣東話解法：原意係水面起漣漪。引申指某種感覺或者影響好似波浪咁擴散、蔓延。廣東話講「起漣漪」、「蔓延」或者「擴散」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: A sense of relief rippled through the crowd.
  • 廣東話口語: 一種鬆一口氣嘅感覺喺人群之中蔓延開去。

18. compelling

  • 詞性：形容詞 (Adjective)
  • 讀音：/kəmˈpel.ɪŋ/
  • 廣東話解法：理由或者故事非常有說服力、吸引人，令人不得不信或者不得不注意。廣東話講「極具說服力」或者「引人入勝」。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: The book provides compelling evidence for its theory.
  • 廣東話口語: 本書為佢嘅理論提供咗極具說服力嘅證據。

19. operant conditioning

  • 詞性：名詞 (Noun)
  • 讀音：/ˈɒp.ər.ənt kənˈdɪʃ.ən.ɪŋ/
  • 廣東話解法：心理學專有名詞，中文譯做「操作制約」或「操作性條件反射」。簡單嚟講就係透過獎勵（增強）同懲罰去改變行為嘅學習過程。
Tip地道廣東話例句
  • English: We learned about B.F. Skinner and his experiments on operant conditioning.
  • 廣東話口語: 我哋學咗斯金納（B.F. Skinner）同埋佢關於操作制約嘅實驗。

item.description:
Introduction: The Goal

Merge Sort is a classic divide-and-conquer algorithm. Our goal is to prove mathematically that its running time scales at .

To do this, we need to translate the algorithm’s code into a mathematical equation, understand the cost of its individual parts, and then solve that equation by visualizing it as a tree. Let’s build this logic step by step.

Step 1: From Code to the “Time Budget” Equation

Before we can calculate the total time, we need a formula that represents the algorithm’s structure. We call this formula , which stands for the total time required to sort an array of elements.

Let’s look at the underlying code logic for MERGE-SORT and assign a cost to each phase:

  1. Divide (Lines 1-2):

    • Code: if p < r, then q = floor((p + r) / 2)
    • The cost: Calculating the middle index is a basic math operation. It takes the same fraction of a second whether the array has 4 items or 4,000,000 items. Because this cost is constant and does not grow with , it is .

  2. Conquer (Lines 3-4):

    • Code: MERGE-SORT(LeftHalf) and MERGE-SORT(RightHalf)
    • The cost: We are splitting an array of elements into two halves of size . If sorting an array takes time, then sorting one half takes . Because we have to sort two halves, the cost is .

  3. Combine (Line 5):

    • Code: MERGE(LeftHalf, RightHalf)
    • The cost: The algorithm zips the two sorted halves back into a single array. As we will prove in the next section, this takes time directly proportional to the number of elements, . Therefore, it costs .

The Resulting Formula

Adding these parts together gives us our foundational time budget:

Because the linear merging work () completely eclipses the tiny constant-time work spent dividing (), we group all the non-recursive work into a single linear term, representing it as (where is just some constant amount of time per element). This gives us our final, clean recurrence relation:

Step 2: Why is the Combine Step Linear ()?

In our formula, we claimed that merging the arrays takes time. Why is this true? Let’s trace a concrete example and count the exact actions the computer takes inside the MERGE procedure.

Imagine merging two sorted halves into a combined array of 6 elements:

  • Left half : [2, 5, 8]
  • Right half : [1, 4, 7]
  • Combined array : [_, _, _, _, _, _] (6 slots to fill)

At each step, the CPU looks at the front items of and , picks the smaller one, writes it to , and advances its pointer.

Step Comparing front items Smaller item Array after placement Work done

2 2 vs 4 2 [1, 2, _, _, _, _] 1 compare + 1 write

4 5 vs 7 5 [1, 2, 4, 5, _, _] 1 compare + 1 write
5 8 vs 7 7 [1, 2, 4, 5, 7, _] 1 compare + 1 write

The Math Behind the Cost

For every single empty slot in array , the computer performs a fixed, simple set of actions. This basic unit of work takes a tiny, constant amount of time, let’s call it . Because there are slots to fill, the CPU performs that unit of work exactly times.

This proves that merging scales perfectly linearly with the data size.

Step 3: Solving the Formula with a Recursion Tree

Now we know our formula is , and we know why. But how do we solve this equation to get the final runtime? We draw it out as a recursion tree to see the workload at every level of the divide-and-conquer process.

To find the total work of the entire algorithm, we need to calculate the “area” of this tree: width (work per level) multiplied by height (number of levels).

The Width: Work Per Level

  • Top level: We start with 1 problem of size . The merge work is just .
  • Level 1: We split into 2 problems of size . The merge work is .
  • Level 2: We split into 4 problems of size . The merge work is .

The Golden Rule

Notice a pattern? When you break a problem in half, you double the number of subproblems (), but you also cut the work per subproblem in half (). The doubling and the halving perfectly cancel out. Therefore, every single level of the tree requires exactly work.

Wait, what about the very bottom leaf nodes (size 1)? Even though an array of 1 element does not need to be sorted, the CPU still has to allocate stack memory, check the base case (if p < r), and return. This takes a constant time, . Since there are exactly leaf nodes at the bottom, their total cost is . The rule holds true all the way to the bottom.
